newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic to stand for federal president.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic to stand for federal president.

text.p: Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic was officially nominated on Thursday to stand for the presidency of Yugoslavia when the five-year mandate of incumbent Zoran Lilic expires on June 25, his party said.

"Milosevic enjoys undivided...trust by the citizens of Serbia and the Socialist Party of Serbia (SPS) has total confidence in him," SPS vice-president Milorad Vucelic said after talks in Montenegro with leaders of its ruling Democratic Party of Socialists (DPS).
Serbia and its tiny ally Montenegro comprise the new Yugoslavia formed after the violent break-up of the former six-member Balkan federation in 1991.
Montenegro's DPS said in a statement it would back Milosevic's nomination but it baulked at an SPS proposal for amendments to the federal constitution.

Vucelic said the amendments were needed to enable Milosevic to be elected by direct ballot and would not affect equality between the two republics, but the fears they would be drafted to give unresticted powers to Milosevic.
"It looks like a marginal change but it could change Montenegro's position in the federation," DPS vice president Milica Pejanovic Djurisic said after five hours of talks with an SPS delegation.
Lilic, the current Yugoslav president, has largely ceremonial powers and was elected by parliament.
Analysts said Milosevic, the real power in Yugoslavia and Serbia, did not want to be held hostage by any parliamentary majority and would seek instead to be elected by popular vote.

He would be counting on his uncontested popularity bolstered by state-run media despite a deteriorating economic situation. He is about to complete his second term as president of Serbia and cannot stand for a third term.
Djurisic belongs to a reformist DPS faction led by Montenegrin Prime Minister Milo Djukanovic which is at odds with hardliners led by Montenegrin President Momir Bulatovic.

Djukanovic, who appears to have won the upper hand over Bulatovic so far, has frequently urged Milosevic to implement the Dayton peace accords to enable sanctions barring Serbia and Montenegro from desperately need foreign funds to be lifted.
He has also managed to privatise a large part of Montenegro's economy whereas Milosevic has been dragging his feet on economic reforms.
